summary: Describes kx509, a protocol that uses Kerberos tickets to obtain X.509 certificates. Where a Kerberos infrastructure already exists, this can involve much less overhead than getting certificates by other means. The document records how the protocol was used in 2012. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you already have a wristband that proves who you are at a park, this lets you swap it for a different kind of pass at another gate without showing all your papers again.

questions: get x509 certificate from kerberos ticket
subtitle: Using Kerberos tickets to request X.509 certificates when Kerberos infrastructure already exists.

tldr.problem: Organizations that deploy both Kerberos (for network authentication) and X.509 certificates (for TLS and other uses) typically require separate credential issuance processes, duplicating administrative work.
tldr.mechanism: The kx509 protocol allows a client that holds a valid Kerberos ticket to request an X.509 certificate from a Kerberized Certificate Authority (KCA) in a single UDP request-reply exchange. The Kerberos ticket authenticates the client; the server verifies the request integrity and issues the certificate.
tldr.outcome: Organizations with existing Kerberos infrastructure can issue X.509 certificates with much less overhead than traditional Certificate Authorities, and the International Grid Trust Federation recognizes these certificates for resource access.

today: RFC 6717 is an Informational RFC documenting the kx509 protocol as used in 2012. It has not been obsoleted. The RFC notes that the IETF Kerberos working group has expected work to address security limitations (especially proof-of-possession) in a future incompatible version of the protocol.

sections.title: The Dual Credential Problem
sections.content:
Most secure IT infrastructure uses two forms of cryptographic identification: Kerberos tickets for network authentication and access, and X.509 certificates for secure web connections (TLS), email signing, and other purposes. Where both systems coexist, the challenge is ensuring that the same person's Kerberos ticket and X.509 certificate refer to the same identity.

Traditionally, acquiring an X.509 certificate requires interaction with a separate Certificate Authority (CA) and involves complex setup. However, if Kerberos infrastructure already exists and a user has a valid Kerberos ticket, why not use that ticket to obtain a corresponding X.509 certificate? This is exactly what the kx509 protocol enables. By leveraging existing Kerberos infrastructure, an organization can issue X.509 certificates with far less overhead than deploying a traditional CA.

The protocol has been deployed at large organizations for years and is recognized by the International Grid Trust Federation (IGTF) as a valid Short Lived Credential Service (SLCS).
sections.eli5: Two common ways to prove who you are on the Internet are Kerberos (fast, for your company network) and X.509 certificates (standard, for web browsers). Instead of asking both systems separately, kx509 lets you show your Kerberos proof to get an X.509 certificate right away.

sections.title: Protocol Structure and Messages
sections.content:
The kx509 protocol operates in a single request-reply exchange over UDP. Both messages begin with a 4-byte version ID (reserved two bytes, then major and minor version numbers; this document defines version 2.0), followed by DER-encoded ASN.1 data.

The request packet contains three elements: (1) a Kerberos AP-REQ (an application request built from a valid service ticket), (2) an HMAC-SHA-1 hash computed over the version ID, AP-REQ, and public key using the Kerberos session key, and (3) the client's public key (DER-encoded RSA key). The public key and its corresponding private key are generated by the client beforehand.

The reply packet contains (1) an error code (0 for success, non-zero for various error conditions), (2) optionally a hash (computed the same way as the request) for integrity verification, (3) optionally a DER-encoded X.509 certificate if the request succeeded, and (4) optionally error text. The server must only return valid combinations: either (error code, hash, certificate) for success, or (error code, hash) if authentication succeeded but certificate generation failed, or (error code, e-text) if authentication failed.
sections.eli5: The client says 'here is my Kerberos ticket and my new public key' in a signed message. The server checks the signature with the Kerberos key, verifies the ticket is real, and sends back a certificate, also signed so the client knows it is real.

sections.title: How a Client Uses the Protocol
sections.content:
Before contacting the server, the client must discover the KCA server's canonical name and port (usually via DNS SRV lookup for _kca._udp._realm_, where _realm_ is the Kerberos realm). The client then generates an RSA public/private key pair and acquires a Kerberos service ticket for the KCA using its Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT), which it typically obtained during login.

The client constructs a kx509 request by encoding the AP-REQ, computing an HMAC-SHA-1 hash of the version ID, AP-REQ, and public key (using the Kerberos session key from the service ticket), and including the DER-encoded public key. This request is sent to the KCA server via UDP.

Upon receiving the request, the server verifies that the AP-REQ is valid and not expired, checks that the HMAC is correct, determines the client's identity from the AP-REQ, and creates an X.509 certificate identifying that principal. If successful, the server sends back the certificate with its own HMAC. The client verifies the returned HMAC before accepting the certificate. If verification fails, the client should not use the certificate.

Defined error codes distinguish permanent client errors (e.g., incompatible version), solvable client errors (e.g., expired credentials), temporary client errors (e.g., packet loss), permanent server errors (e.g., misconfiguration), and temporary server errors (e.g., server overload).
sections.eli5: The client looks up the server, gets a Kerberos ticket for it, makes a public key, sends a signed message with the ticket and key, and the server sends back a signed certificate. Done.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limitations
sections.content:
The protocol relies entirely on Kerberos for encryption and authentication. All security properties of the Kerberos realm apply: if an attacker compromises Kerberos keys or tickets, they can request certificates in other users' names.

A critical limitation is that the public key in the request is sent in the clear, without any proof that the requester actually possesses the corresponding private key. This means an eavesdropper could request a certificate with someone else's public key and claim to have created signatures with that key. The RFC states that the certificate should only be used in contexts where the identity of the requester is unimportant or where the subsequent use of the certificate independently proves possession of the private key (e.g., TLS Certificate Verify messages contain signatures that prove key ownership).

Additionally, X.509 certificates typically have longer validity periods than Kerberos tickets. The RFC recommends that the certificate validity should not exceed the predecessor Kerberos ticket's lifetime unless local policy clearly allows it. This prevents the certificate from being used after the Kerberos infrastructure has revoked the underlying ticket.

The protocol does not address certificate verification, path construction, or revocation; applications must handle these independently. A future version of the protocol is expected to add proof-of-possession mechanisms and other security improvements.
sections.eli5: The Kerberos ticket proves you to the server, but the server cannot be sure you have the private key. A future version will fix this. Also, the certificate should not stay valid longer than your Kerberos ticket.

sections.title: Deployment and Practical Use
sections.content:
The protocol is conventionally run on UDP port 9878, registered with IANA as the 'kca-service'. Many organizations store kx509-issued certificates in the Kerberos credential cache alongside tickets, and use PKCS#11 libraries to make them accessible to standard PKI applications like web browsers.

The protocol supports RSA keys; a future version is expected to add algorithm agility. Appendix A discusses certificate caching and deployment considerations, noting that since kx509 certificates inherit the Kerberos ticket's lifetime, they should typically be deleted when supporting tickets are deleted.

The RFC documents historic extensions to the protocol that are no longer in use, including DSA key support and provisions for arbitrary client version information to be embedded in certificates.

Real deployments at large organizations and universities demonstrate that the protocol is practical and stable. Certificates issued via kx509 are accepted by tools that need X.509 certificates, including the Grid infrastructure for scientific computing.
sections.eli5: The protocol runs on port 9878. In practice, certificates sit next to Kerberos tickets in a shared cache, and applications access them through standard certificate APIs. Organizations have been using it for many years with good results.
